fields.title: The Economics of Reliability
fields.keyTakeaway: Investments in reliability pay off as long as they cost less than the damage prevented, and reducing detection time usually yields a better return per ruble than redundancy.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: How do you know when to stop investing in reliability?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Reliability is the only area where it is easy to spend infinitely and impossible to reach perfection. Without a stopping criterion, the team will either underinvest or turn reliability into an end in itself.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: The comparison is simple: **[[cost-of-downtime|cost of downtime]] vs. cost of prevention.**
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: The cost of downtime is calculated using peak hour revenue, the share of affected scenarios, and the unrecoverable portion. The latter is important: some orders not placed during an outage will be placed afterward. Deferred revenue is not a loss.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: The cost of prevention is team effort plus infrastructure plus ongoing operations. The latter is often forgotten: cross-zone redundancy costs not just a quarter of work, but also a monthly bill and added complexity for every future change.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: [[term-3|The break-even point]] lies where the next nine costs more than the damage prevented.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: What is not in the arithmetic and must be considered separately:
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: *Reputation.* A public outage costs more than missed revenue. Especially at an early product stage. *Contractual obligations.* SLA penalties are direct money. *Internal trust.* A product that "keeps going down" loses support.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: And the flip side: **excessive reliability also has a price** — not just money, but velocity. A team investing in the fifth nine is not building the product.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Calculation for the cross-zone redundancy decision.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: Cost of an hour of downtime during evening peak: about 1 800 orders, commission ~4%, average ticket 2 400 — roughly 170 thousand rubles. Non-recoverable share based on past incidents is about 60%. Total ~100 thousand per hour.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Over half a year there were 4 incidents totaling 85 minutes, including 40 minutes at peak. Damage — about 70 thousand over half a year.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Cross-zone redundancy: a quarter of work (about 3m in team cost) plus 400 thousand a month. Over half a year — 5.4m versus the preventable 70 thousand.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: The decision is obvious: it does not pay off by orders of magnitude. Instead, the same money went into reducing detection time — alerts, on-call rotation, automated checks. This cut the average incident duration from 21 minutes to 8, yielding 60% of the effect for 5% of the cost.
fields.sections/3/blocks/5/text: We ran a separate calculation for the corporate tier: compensation comes into play there, and the arithmetic changes. But even that did not make redundancy profitable given the current number of corporate clients.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: The calculation does not work for catastrophic scenarios: data loss or a leak cannot be measured in lost revenue. Decisions for them are made not by payback, but by acceptability.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Investments in reliability pay off as long as they cost less than the damage they prevent, and reducing detection time usually yields a higher return per ruble than redundancy.
